title: Connie's Inn with Armstrong and the Fleischmann Yeast broadcasts
summary: With Armstrong at Connie's Inn the band played three shows nightly, rehearsed after hours and for the radio program, and earned extra pay for rehearsals and broadcasts.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: When we was workin' down there with Louis... It wasn't exactly the Cotton Club then. It was the Cotton Club later, but it opened up as Connie's Inn downtown. It was called Connie's Inn. You worked the same hours. At this time, Louis was doing a radio show for Fleischman Yeast, the Fleischman Yeast program. Now, we had to squeeze time in there in the daytime to rehearse the Fleischman Yeast show.

We had to rehearse that to be broadcast. And you talk about somebody not having enough time, we did not have enough time to rehearse one thing and then another. We was blowin'- blowin'-blowin' all of the time.

It was really a tough thing. You're going to work at six o'clock, you're playing three shows until two or three o'clock in the morning, then you're rehearsing after the show until seven o'clock in the morning. Then during the day, you've got to rehearse the radio program. It just wasn't worth it. It was rough. It was really rough.
Louis never complained about anything, and he blew his head off. I mean, he had more stamina than anybody I ever seen in my life. He had it.

And we worked down there, Connie's Inn... Oh, we were there six months the first time. Then the second time we were there, we went out on the road after being there three weeks, and we started doing the broadcasts from different cities, like Chicago, the big cities we'd run into all the way out to California.

But we survived it. It was pretty nice. I mean, that made the pocketbook kind of heavy there, when you're collecting from all these different things. Like, we were getting paid for rehearsals, which we didn't get before, and we were getting paid for the broadcasts, which was extra.
That was good. That was very good. Plus, the regular show, I mean the regular job, which was hard... That was hard. That was a hard job. But when you put it all together, I guess it was good.

My wife and I, we had a little hard time in between there, because she could not believe anybody was blowin' their horn as often and as much as I said I was at Connie's Inn, rehearsing and this-that-and-the-other. She couldn't believe anybody was rehearsing that much. And I guess the other fellows had the same trouble, too. It was tough on a wife. Real tough on a wife. But, that's the business. What are you gonna do? It wasn't the only band. There was other bands working under different strenuous conditions, too. And that was life. That was the way it was.
I guess Small's Paradise was no different.
Well, Small's Paradise, they didn't go through all that rigmarole. They had a show. They put on a show twice a night.
